question: When overtaking a cyclist at up to 30 mph, what minimum passing distance does the Highway Code recommend?
options: At least 0.5 metres
At least 1 metre
At least 1.5 metres
At least 3 metres
explanation: Overtake only when it is safe and legal to do so. Give motorcyclists, cyclists and horse riders at least as much room as you would when overtaking a car (at least 1.5 metres for cyclists at speeds up to 30 mph, more at higher speeds; at least 2 metres for horse riders, passing at no more than 10 mph). (Highway Code rule 163.)

question: When passing a horse and rider, what speed and clearance does the Highway Code advise?
options: Any speed if you sound your horn first
30 mph if the road is straight
No more than 10 mph, leaving at least 2 metres of space
No more than 20 mph, leaving 1 metre
explanation: Overtake only when it is safe and legal to do so. Give motorcyclists, cyclists and horse riders at least as much room as you would when overtaking a car (at least 1.5 metres for cyclists at speeds up to 30 mph, more at higher speeds; at least 2 metres for horse riders, passing at no more than 10 mph). (Highway Code rule 163.)

question: You are turning into a side road. Pedestrians are waiting to cross at the junction. What should you do?
options: Give way to them — they have priority
Sound your horn and continue
Wave them across
Stop only if they have already stepped into the road
explanation: Take extra care at junctions. You should give way to pedestrians crossing or waiting to cross a road into which or from which you are turning. Watch out for cyclists, motorcyclists and powered wheelchairs/mobility scooters. Watch out for long vehicles which may have to take a different course. (Highway Code rule 170.)

question: At traffic lights, what is the area marked between the two stop lines for?
options: A pedestrian refuge
A bus-only waiting area
To allow cyclists to position themselves ahead of other traffic
A loading bay
explanation: Advanced stop lines allow cycles to be positioned ahead of other traffic. Motorists, including motorcyclists, MUST stop at the first white line reached if the lights are amber or red and should avoid blocking the way or encroaching on the marked area at other times. (Highway Code rule 178.)

question: A pedestrian is waiting at a zebra crossing. What does the Highway Code say you should do?
options: Sound your horn so they wait
Wave them across
Continue — they only have priority once on the crossing
Slow down and give way to them
explanation: Zebra and parallel crossings. As you approach, look out for pedestrians waiting to cross and be ready to slow down or stop to let them cross. You should give way to pedestrians waiting to cross and MUST give way when a pedestrian has moved onto a crossing. (Highway Code rule 195.)

question: At a pelican crossing the amber light is flashing. What MUST you do?
options: Sound your horn to warn pedestrians
Give way to any pedestrians still on the crossing
Drive on — flashing amber means go
Stop and wait for green
explanation: Pelican crossings. These are signal-controlled crossings where flashing amber follows the red 'Stop' light. You MUST stop when the red light shows. When the amber light is flashing, you MUST give way to any pedestrians on the crossing. (Highway Code rule 196.)

question: How does the light sequence at a puffin crossing differ from a pelican crossing?
options: There are two green phases
Red and amber show together before red
There is no flashing amber phase — the sequence is the same as ordinary traffic lights
A flashing green man is shown to drivers
explanation: Toucan, puffin and equestrian crossings. These are similar to pelican crossings, but there is no flashing amber phase; the light sequence is the same as at traffic lights. (Highway Code rule 199.)

question: According to the Highway Code, which road users are most at risk from road traffic?
options: Lorry and bus drivers
Drivers of older vehicles
Pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists and horse riders
Drivers of small cars
explanation: The road users most at risk from road traffic are pedestrians, in particular children, older adults and disabled people, cyclists, horse riders and motorcyclists. It is particularly important to be aware of them and give them plenty of room. (Highway Code rule 204.)

question: A pedestrian is carrying a white cane with a red band. What does this tell you?
options: They are a doctor on call
They have a learning disability
They are deaf as well as blind
They are blind only
explanation: Particularly vulnerable pedestrians include children and older pedestrians who may not be able to judge your speed, people with disabilities, blind or partially sighted people who may be carrying a white cane or using a guide dog, and deafblind people who may be carrying a white cane with a red band. (Highway Code rule 207.)

question: A school crossing patrol steps into the road and shows a “Stop — children” sign. What MUST you do?
options: Stop only if children are visible
Slow down and pass with care
Stop — it is an offence not to
Sound your horn and continue
explanation: You MUST stop when a school crossing patrol shows a 'Stop for children' sign. (Highway Code rule 210.)

question: When passing animals on the road, what should you avoid doing?
options: Being prepared to stop
Slowing down
Giving them plenty of room
Sounding your horn, revving your engine or accelerating rapidly
explanation: Animals. When passing animals, drive slowly. Give them plenty of room and be ready to stop. Do not scare animals by sounding your horn, revving your engine or accelerating rapidly once you have passed them. (Highway Code rule 214.)

question: You are overtaking a horse and rider. What clearance and speed does the Highway Code advise?
options: At least 2 metres of space and a maximum speed of 10 mph
Any clearance if the road is straight
1 metre and 20 mph
1.5 metres and 30 mph
explanation: Horse riders and horse-drawn vehicles. Be particularly careful of horse riders and horse-drawn vehicles especially when overtaking. Always pass wide (at least 2 metres) and slowly (no more than 10 mph). Look out for horse riders' and horse drivers' signals and heed a request to slow down or stop. (Highway Code rule 215.)

question: The Highway Code recommends opening your car door with the hand furthest from it (the “Dutch Reach”). Why?
options: It prevents the door swinging fully open
It is required by law
It uses less effort
It makes you turn and look for cyclists and other traffic before opening the door
explanation: Use off-street parking areas, or bays marked out with white lines on the road as parking places, wherever possible. Stop as close as you can to the side. You MUST switch off the engine, headlights and fog lights, apply the handbrake before leaving the vehicle, and ensure you do not hit anyone when you open your door — check for cyclists or other traffic by using your mirrors and looking round (the 'Dutch Reach'). (Highway Code rule 239.)

question: Highway Code rule 3 is about “rules for pedestrians”. Which statement is taken from this rule?
options: Help other road users to see you.
Where there are barriers, cross the road only at the gaps provided for pedestrians.
At traffic lights, there may be special signals for pedestrians.
Toucan crossings are light-controlled crossings which allow cyclists and pedestrians to share crossing space and cross at the same time.
explanation: Help other road users to see you. Wear or carry something light-coloured, bright or fluorescent in poor daylight conditions. When it is dark, use reflective materials (e.g. armbands, sashes, waistcoats, jackets, footwear), which can be seen by drivers using headlights up to three times as far away as non-reflective materials. (Highway Code rule 3.)
